paragraphs: Multilevel optimization involves nested decisions: solving one optimization problem depends on the solutions of problems below it. Although applications had been discussed for decades, methods largely addressed only two levels. This paper develops a gradient-based method for problems with an arbitrary number of levels, extending an approach previously used for bilevel optimization.

The starting idea is to replace a lower-level optimization problem with a fixed sequence of steepest-descent updates. This makes the lower-level computation part of the reformulated problem. The authors extend this construction across multiple levels and prove that their reformulation approaches the original multilevel problem asymptotically. That guarantee concerns the limiting reformulation, rather than exact equivalence after any fixed number of updates.

The experiments examine a three-level hyperparameter-learning model that accounts for data poisoning. In noisy-data settings, it produces more stable predictions than an existing two-level model. This finding supports the usefulness of the additional optimization level in the tested setting, while the broader contribution is a method with theoretical support for optimization beyond two nested levels.
neurips-2021-a-gradient-method-for-multi.tldr: A gradient-based method extends optimization to multiple nested levels, with an asymptotic reformulation guarantee and improved prediction stability in a tested three-level application.

paragraphs: Blind source separation asks how to recover underlying signals from their mixtures. Independent component analysis is a common approach for linear mixtures, but a signal-processing algorithm does not automatically provide a plausible account of a biological circuit. This paper develops an ICA objective designed to support both a neural architecture and biologically plausible learning rules.

Two requirements guide the construction. The network must process samples as they arrive, recovering sources without retaining a substantial portion of the dataset. Its synaptic updates must also depend on variables available near each synapse. Deriving the architecture and learning rules from an objective connects the circuit's computations to the source-separation problem it is intended to solve.

A distinctive feature is that total output-neuron activity modulates synaptic plasticity. The authors suggest several possible biological carriers for this modulation, including neuromodulators, extracellular calcium, local field potentials, and nitric oxide. These are possible implementations, not established explanations of how the brain performs separation. The contribution is a mathematically motivated candidate algorithm that accommodates the stated online and local-learning requirements.
neurips-2021-a-normative-and-biologicall.tldr: The paper derives an online ICA neural network with local learning rules and output-activity modulation that could plausibly be implemented biologically.

paragraphs: This paper studies stochastic optimization when each update uses a minibatch of gradient estimates. Its setting is smooth optimization with convex or strongly convex objectives. The central question is how convergence can benefit simultaneously from larger minibatches and a smaller minimum expected loss, rather than obtaining a favorable dependence on only one of these quantities.

The proposed algorithm is analyzed as optimal in its dependence on both quantities at once. The comparison with earlier methods identifies distinct shortcomings: one method does not adapt to the minimum expected loss, another has a weaker dependence on minibatch size, and a third both has that weaker dependence and applies only to least-squares problems.

For interpolation learning, the improved minibatch dependence yields a linear parallelization speedup where the compared methods yield a square-root speedup. This gives the theoretical improvement a concrete computational interpretation: increasing parallel work can translate more effectively into optimization progress in that setting. The claim is about the stated optimization regime and parameter dependence, rather than a guarantee of linear hardware speedups for arbitrary learning problems.
neurips-2021-an-even-more-optimal-stocha.tldr: A stochastic optimization algorithm achieves jointly optimal dependence on minibatch size and minimum expected loss, yielding linear parallelization speedups in interpolation learning.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks often contain many repeated blocks, making parameter sharing an appealing way to reduce model size. Simply reusing parameters can, however, restrict what the network represents and cause gradients to shrink or grow excessively during training. This paper redesigns the convolution block and its training procedure to address those problems together.

The method separates out a filter basis that can be learned and reused across blocks. The authors show that making the basis elements orthonormal can control the problematic gradient behavior. They also introduce an orthogonality regularizer and empirically show that it improves gradient flow. The shared component is therefore paired with a training mechanism intended to keep recursive reuse manageable.

On image classification and object detection experiments, the proposed networks save substantial numbers of parameters while consistently outperforming their overparameterized counterparts. In these tests, sharing does more than preserve performance in a smaller model: the block design and regularization also improve representation capability. The results support this particular combination of structured sharing and gradient control, rather than parameter reuse alone.
neurips-2021-deeply-shared-filter-bases-.tldr: Sharing learned filter bases with orthogonality regularization reduces CNN parameters while improving gradient flow and performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: To study networks spanning brain regions, researchers often calculate measures of neural activity and then use linear factor models to uncover shared structure. Measures such as power spectra fit this workflow, but directed communication between regions has been harder to include. Existing directional measures conflict with assumptions implicit in the factor-model approach.

The paper introduces Directed Spectrum, a spectral measure of directed communication. Its central theoretical contribution is a proof that this measure is compatible with the relevant assumptions of linear factor models. The authors also provide an estimation method, connecting the mathematical definition to a quantity that can be obtained from neural recordings.

Experiments with simulated data and real neural recordings show that factor models using Directed Spectrum better capture underlying brain networks than the alternatives considered. The approach matters because direction of communication becomes an explicit part of the network representation. It allows the established linear-factor workflow to incorporate information about communication between neural populations, alongside the broader aim of identifying the networks involved in computation.
neurips-2021-directed-spectrum-measures-.tldr: Directed Spectrum makes directed neural communication compatible with linear factor models and improves network recovery in simulated and real recording data.

paragraphs: Distribution-free prediction guarantees do not automatically provide confidence intervals for an underlying regression function. The distinction is between predicting an outcome and estimating a quantity such as the average outcome conditional on the features. This paper investigates when confidence intervals for that conditional mean can become increasingly precise without relying on distributional assumptions.

The abstract describes two contrasting endpoints. With continuously distributed features, previous results show that valid confidence intervals cannot have widths that vanish as the sample grows. When features take only a small number of values, inference is straightforward. The paper studies the intermediate settings, where the feature distribution is neither a small finite collection nor the continuous extreme.

The authors identify several regimes and characterize the possibility of shrinking intervals through effective support size. In the settings studied, vanishing width is achievable if and only if this size is smaller than the square of the sample size. This establishes a boundary for distribution-free regression inference: the relevant comparison involves how broadly feature values are distributed relative to the available data.
neurips-2021-distribution-free-inference.tldr: The paper characterizes when distribution-free confidence intervals for regression can shrink, using effective feature-support size relative to squared sample size.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks commonly build representations around nodes and their connections, but some tasks require rich representations of the edges themselves. This matters for reconstructing or generating graphs, and for classification when edges carry distinguishing information. The paper develops a framework that makes edge information a central part of graph representation learning.

Its main construction, Dual Hypergraph Transformation, turns the original graph's edges into nodes of a hypergraph. This lets message-passing methods normally used to represent nodes operate on the original edges. After learning those representations, the method clusters or removes edges to produce a graph-level summary built from edge information.

Across the tested graph datasets, the method substantially outperforms existing approaches on representation and generation tasks. Its pooling method also outperforms the compared state-of-the-art pooling methods on graph classification. The authors attribute these results to accurate edge representations, lossless compression of nodes, and removal of irrelevant edges for more effective message passing. The contribution connects edge learning and graph summarization within the same transformed representation.
neurips-2021-edge-representation-learnin.tldr: Transforming graph edges into hypergraph nodes enables edge-focused message passing and pooling that improve the reported graph-learning results.

paragraphs: Extreme multi-label text classification selects relevant labels for a text from a very large collection. Recommendation, document tagging, and semantic search can all take this form. Transformer-based methods improve classification quality, but adapting their text representations to an enormous label space can require lengthy training even on powerful graphics processors.

XR-Transformer addresses that cost through recursive fine-tuning. It trains transformer models on a sequence of objectives at different resolutions, each related to the original classification objective. The central change is therefore how the model is adapted to the label space: the training process works through related resolutions instead of treating the full task as a single fine-tuning objective.

The experiments report substantially shorter training times together with improved state-of-the-art results. On Amazon-3M, which contains three million labels, XR-Transformer is 20 times faster than X-Transformer and raises Precision@1 from 51% to 54%. That comparison shows that the reported efficiency gain does not require sacrificing top-ranked prediction quality. It supports multi-resolution fine-tuning as an effective approach for the evaluated large-label classification problems.
neurips-2021-fast-multi-resolution-trans.tldr: XR-Transformer uses recursive multi-resolution fine-tuning to reduce training time while improving extreme multi-label text classification accuracy.

paragraphs: Double Q-learning helps address the overestimation problem associated with Q-learning and has been successful in practice. Its theoretical convergence behavior has been less well understood. This paper strengthens that understanding by analyzing a constant learning rate, a more challenging case than the polynomially changing rate used in the previous finite-time analysis.

The authors develop analytical tools for both synchronous and asynchronous double Q-learning. They characterize the time needed to reach a globally optimal solution within a specified accuracy. The results track accuracy, the discount factor, and either the number of state-action pairs or a parameter describing the asynchronous sampling strategy.

The reported rates improve the previous dependence on all of these major parameters by orders of magnitude. This matters because a finite-time analysis connects learning progress to a concrete amount of computation, rather than describing convergence only in the limit. The work provides stronger theoretical support for fast double Q-learning under the analyzed updates, while retaining explicit dependence on how accuracy, discounting, problem size, and sampling affect convergence.
neurips-2021-faster-non-asymptotic-conve.tldr: New analysis gives substantially improved finite-time convergence rates for synchronous and asynchronous double Q-learning with a constant learning rate.

paragraphs: Dense visual prediction requires representations that preserve spatial detail, as in locating human poses or assigning semantic labels across an image. HRFormer is designed to learn high-resolution representations for these tasks. Its motivation is that the original Vision Transformer produces lower-resolution representations while imposing substantial memory and computation costs.

The architecture combines parallel processing at multiple resolutions, drawing on HRNet, with self-attention inside small, non-overlapping image windows. Restricting attention to these windows improves efficiency, but separates their attention computations. To exchange information across the window boundaries, the authors add a convolution to the feed-forward network. The design therefore addresses both local processing cost and communication between windows.

The paper demonstrates effectiveness on human pose estimation and semantic segmentation. In the stated COCO pose comparison, HRFormer exceeds Swin Transformer by 1.3 AP while using 50% fewer parameters and 30% fewer FLOPs. These results support the architecture's ability to combine detailed spatial representations with efficient computation in the evaluated tasks, rather than requiring a larger model to obtain the reported improvement.
neurips-2021-hrformer-high-resolution-vi.tldr: HRFormer combines parallel multi-resolution features, local attention, and cross-window convolution to improve dense prediction with lower reported model and computation costs.

paragraphs: A stochastic multi-armed bandit problem involves choosing repeatedly among options whose rewards are uncertain. This paper studies a structured version in which reward distributions belong to a one-dimensional exponential family and the options have a unimodal structure. That structure provides information an algorithm can exploit when searching for the best option.

The authors introduce IMED-UB by adapting the Indexed Minimum Empirical Divergence algorithm to the unimodal setting. Their contribution is both an algorithm and an analysis showing that it exploits the structure optimally in the asymptotic sense. A concise finite-time analysis establishes behavior over a finite number of decisions and yields the asymptotic optimality result.

Numerical experiments show that IMED-UB compares favorably with recent state-of-the-art algorithms. The empirical finding complements the theoretical guarantee: the method is competitive in the tested problems as well as optimally adapted to the stated structure in the limit. The distributional family and unimodality are central to this result, defining the setting in which the algorithm's structural advantage and guarantees apply.
neurips-2021-indexed-minimum-empirical-d.tldr: IMED-UB exploits unimodal bandit structure with a finite-time analysis yielding asymptotic optimality and favorable numerical comparisons.

paragraphs: Large physical systems can contain billions of interacting elements, making both forward simulation and learning dynamics from data computationally demanding. LSH-SMILE provides a shared framework for accelerating these two operations. It exploits the locality of partial differential equation updates and the fact that multiple elements can exhibit similar behavior over time.

The method uses locality-sensitive hashing to group elements with similar dynamics into buckets and process their updates together. Its computation scales with the number of occupied buckets rather than treating every element's update separately. The potential saving comes from repeated dynamics: elements that behave similarly can share update work within the framework.

The authors prove a bound on the approximation errors introduced by this grouping. In experiments, simulations achieve quality comparable to exact approaches while requiring substantially less time and space. Those savings also improve learning performance by allowing gradients to propagate over longer durations. The contribution therefore links efficient simulation to better learning of dynamics, with both a theoretical error analysis and empirical evidence for the benefits of grouped computation.
neurips-2021-lsh-smile-locality-sensitiv.tldr: LSH-SMILE groups elements with similar dynamics to accelerate physical simulation and learning, with an error bound and comparable simulation quality in experiments.

paragraphs: Evaluating a generative model involves comparing generated data with the structure of the target data. This paper approaches that comparison through the topology of the manifolds on which two distributions concentrate. Its goal is to detect structural differences across multiple scales, including discrepancies that reflect missing or distorted parts of the generated distribution.

The central tool, Cross-Barcode, tracks these multiscale discrepancies for a pair of distributions in a high-dimensional space. The authors turn this tool into the Manifold Topology Divergence score and evaluate it across images, three-dimensional shapes, and time series. The method does not depend on pretrained networks and is designed to work across domains.

The experiments show detection of different degrees of mode dropping, collapse within modes, invented modes, and image disturbance. The algorithm also scales essentially linearly with ambient dimension. Together, these findings support a broadly applicable topology-based assessment tool: it can distinguish several forms of generative failure while accommodating varied data dimensions and types, without requiring a domain-specific pretrained representation.
neurips-2021-manifold-topology-divergenc.tldr: Manifold Topology Divergence compares multiscale data structure to detect generative-model failures across domains without pretrained networks.

paragraphs: Meta-learning uses experience across training tasks to improve learning on new tasks. Uniformly sampling those tasks treats them as equally useful, which can be problematic when a limited task collection contains noise or imbalance. This paper proposes an adaptive task scheduler to reduce the influence of detrimental tasks and prevent majority tasks from dominating training.

The scheduler is a neural model that predicts sampling probabilities for candidate tasks. It uses two factors related to the current meta-model that characterize task difficulty, and it is trained to improve generalization to unseen tasks. The authors also show theoretically that accounting for these factors improves the meta-training loss and the optimization landscape.

Under noisy meta-learning conditions and limited budgets, the reported gains over state-of-the-art schedulers reach 13% on miniImageNet and 18% on a drug-discovery benchmark. These are maximum reported improvements in the studied settings. The findings support treating task selection as a learned part of meta-training, with usefulness assessed in relation to the current model and its ability to transfer to new tasks.
neurips-2021-meta-learning-with-an-adapt.tldr: A learned task scheduler improves meta-learning under noise and limited budgets by adapting task sampling to the current model.

paragraphs: Streaming active learning requires a learner to decide which arriving examples deserve a label request. This paper studies that problem with stochastic labels in a nonparametric setting, without assumptions on the class of labeling functions. The challenge is to control prediction performance and label use when the complexity of the function being learned is unknown.

The method uses neural tangent kernel approximation tools to construct a neural embedding. That embedding defines the feature space and the model learned on top of it. Because the label-request threshold depends closely on function complexity, the authors also develop a version that needs no prior complexity knowledge. It uses regret balancing to handle the resulting online model-selection problem efficiently.

The analysis gives joint guarantees on cumulative regret and the number of labels requested, with both depending on the complexity of the actual labeling function. In the linear case, the guarantees recover known minimax relationships between generalization error and label complexity. This connects the neural construction to established optimal results while addressing adaptation to unknown complexity in the broader setting.
neurips-2021-neural-active-learning-with.tldr: A neural streaming active-learning method adapts to unknown labeling complexity while providing joint guarantees on regret and label requests.

paragraphs: NeuroLKH combines a learned graph model with the established Lin-Kernighan-Helsgaun heuristic for the Traveling Salesman Problem. The approach uses learning to guide the heuristic's search. Its central premise is that a neural model can supply useful choices and adjustments within an already strong routing algorithm.

A Sparse Graph Network learns two outputs through different training signals: supervised learning produces edge scores, while unsupervised learning produces node penalties. NeuroLKH uses these outputs to construct candidate edges and transform edge distances. Both changes shape the search performed by LKH, linking the network's predictions directly to decisions made by the traditional solver.

The experiments show that a single model trained across a range of problem sizes significantly outperforms LKH and generalizes well to much larger instances. The authors also demonstrate applicability to capacitated vehicle routing, pickup and delivery, and capacitated routing with time windows. These findings support the value of learning search guidance that works across instance sizes and can be incorporated into several related routing problems.
neurips-2021-neurolkh-combining-deep-lea.tldr: NeuroLKH learns edge scores and node penalties to guide LKH search, improving reported routing results and generalizing to larger instances.

paragraphs: This paper asks how robust sequential decision-making can be when an adversary corrupts losses in an otherwise stochastic setting. It considers prediction with expert advice and multi-armed bandits. The objective is to characterize the unavoidable performance cost of corruption, rather than merely show that a particular algorithm tolerates some corrupted observations.

For expert prediction, the authors analyze anytime Hedge with decreasing learning rates and algorithms satisfying second-order regret bounds. Their regret guarantee combines an uncorrupted term depending on the number of experts and the gap parameter with an additional term growing as the square root of the corruption level. Thus, corruption enters the guarantee through a sublinear dependence.

A matching lower bound shows that the expert-prediction guarantee is tight up to a constant factor. This establishes that the square-root corruption dependence captures optimal robustness in the studied setting. For multi-armed bandits, the paper separately supplies a lower bound that is nearly tight, differing by a logarithmic factor. The two results have different precision, but both clarify fundamental limits on robustness.
neurips-2021-on-optimal-robustness-to-ad.tldr: The paper establishes optimal square-root corruption dependence for expert prediction and a nearly tight lower bound for corrupted stochastic bandits.

paragraphs: Multilingual question answering is difficult when a language lacks annotated examples or its own knowledge sources. CORA addresses this with a unified model that can retrieve information across languages and answer in the requested language. This allows a question's useful evidence to come from sources beyond those written in that same language.

The system pairs a new cross-lingual dense passage retriever with a multilingual autoregressive answer generator. It produces answers directly in the target language without separate translation or in-language retrieval modules. An iterative training procedure also extends annotations available in high-resource languages to low-resource languages automatically, helping broaden the model's training coverage.

On multilingual open question-answering benchmarks covering 26 languages, CORA substantially improves on the previous state of the art. Nine evaluated languages were unseen during training. The authors' analyses emphasize the contribution of both cross-lingual retrieval and multilingual generation, especially in low-resource settings. The results support sharing access to knowledge and answer-generation capabilities across languages within one system, including cases without language-specific training annotations.
neurips-2021-one-question-answering-mode.tldr: CORA combines cross-lingual retrieval and multilingual generation to answer questions across 26 evaluated languages, including nine unseen during training.

paragraphs: When a function's domain is enormous compared with the evaluation budget, finding its global optimum can be impossible. This paper studies what Gaussian-process optimization can still achieve in that situation. It shifts attention to the quality of the value returned after limited evaluations, rather than requiring the search to reach the absolute best point.

The authors derive upper bounds on Bayesian simple regret, a measure of the returned solution's suboptimality. Their strategies are closely related to expected improvement and upper confidence bound methods. The bounds connect performance to the number of evaluations and domain scale, expressed through cardinality for finite domains and a covariance-function Lipschitz constant for continuous domains.

The results show that useful function values remain attainable even when the evaluation budget is far too small to locate the global optimum. One stated form of usefulness is attaining a certain ratio to the optimal value. The contribution is therefore a quantitative account of partial success: it relates limited search effort to achievable solution quality in domains where exact global optimization is out of reach.
neurips-2021-regret-bounds-for-gaussian-.tldr: Regret bounds show how Gaussian-process optimization can find useful values even when the domain is too large to locate the global optimum.

paragraphs: Autoencoders learn compact representations of complex data, but generating samples also requires control over how those representations are distributed. The paper contrasts a simple unimodal Gaussian prior and challenging variational training with deterministic regularized autoencoders. The latter are easier to train, yet their weak distributional control can require density estimation after training to obtain comparable samples.

The proposed framework uses Gaussian-mixture regularization to shape the latent space during end-to-end deterministic training. Its aim is to accommodate expressive distributions with multiple modes while directly controlling the representation's distribution. This integrates the shaping process into learning, addressing the need to fit a suitable latent density only after the autoencoder has been trained.

The authors state that the training procedure provides direct evidence about whether the latent distribution adequately captures complex aspects of encoded data. Experiments in challenging continuous and discrete domains demonstrate the model's expressiveness and sample quality. The contribution combines simpler deterministic autoencoding with a richer, explicitly shaped latent distribution, tying representation learning more closely to the distribution used for generation.
neurips-2021-shape-your-space-a-gaussian.tldr: Gaussian-mixture regularization shapes a deterministic autoencoder's latent distribution during training, supporting expressive representations and sample generation.

paragraphs: Navigation instructions often mix descriptions of places with references to particular objects. A scene such as a bedroom provides context, while an object such as a green chair supplies a more specific visual cue. SOAT builds a transformer-based navigation agent around these two kinds of information so that its visual representations match the language it must follow.

The agent uses a scene-classification network and an object detector as separate visual encoders. Scene features provide high-level context that supports object processing. This architecture also enables the model to benefit from vision-and-language pretraining, which learns alignment between images and text using large-scale web data.

The reported improvements are 1.8 percentage points in SPL on Room-to-Room and 3.7 percentage points in success rate on Room-Across-Room. Instructions containing at least six object references show still larger gains. That analysis suggests that the model makes better use of object features and connects them more effectively to the instruction text. The evidence supports combining scene context with explicit object information for the evaluated navigation tasks.
neurips-2021-soat-a-scene-and-object-awa.tldr: SOAT combines scene context and object features to improve language-guided navigation, with larger reported gains on instructions containing many object references.

paragraphs: Bandit algorithms collect data adaptively: the choices made during collection respond to earlier observations. Researchers may then want to use those data to answer scientific questions about outcomes or interventions. Classical statistical procedures can fail to produce valid confidence intervals in this setting, making ordinary analysis of the resulting dataset unreliable.

The paper develops inference theory for M-estimators on adaptively collected data, including data from contextual bandits. This broad estimator family includes empirical-risk minimization and maximum likelihood. The key modification is to apply particular adaptive weights, allowing the estimation procedure to account for the adaptive collection process when constructing confidence regions.

The authors prove that these modified estimators yield asymptotically valid confidence regions for a variety of inferential targets. The asymptotic qualification means that validity is established as sample size grows. The contribution extends beyond earlier approaches centered on simple comparisons of means, providing a more general foundation for inference with richer models. This helps connect sequential decision-making datasets to the scientific questions researchers want those datasets to answer.
neurips-2021-statistical-inference-with-.tldr: Adaptively weighted M-estimators provide asymptotically valid confidence regions for a range of targets using data collected by adaptive algorithms.

paragraphs: In distributed optimization, separate machines hold different functions and cooperate to minimize their sum. Computation is only part of the cost: the machines must also exchange information. This paper studies the total number of communicated bits needed to reach a specified additive error when communication occurs directly between pairs of machines.

The main result is an unconditional communication lower bound that applies to deterministic and randomized algorithms without restricting their structure. It relates necessary communication to the number of machines, function dimension, and error tolerance. This breadth matters because the bound is not limited to a particular gradient-descent implementation or a prescribed pattern of algorithmic steps.

Under certain restrictions on parameter values, the lower bound is tight. For quadratic objectives, the authors also develop and analyze a quantized gradient-descent variant that matches the bound within constant factors. The work thus connects an impossibility result with an achievable communication cost in the stated setting. It brings tools from communication complexity into distributed optimization to identify which communication savings are fundamentally attainable.
neurips-2021-towards-tight-communication.tldr: The paper establishes algorithm-independent communication lower bounds for distributed optimization and matches them in specified settings with quantized gradient descent.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns a policy from a fixed dataset, but value estimates can be unreliable for decisions outside that dataset's coverage. Existing approaches often constrain the policy to remain near observed behavior. The paper argues that these methods can require difficult distribution-estimation steps and can also keep the policy unnecessarily close to the data.

The proposed approach uses confidence in Q-value predictions to guide conservatism without estimating or sampling the data distribution. The authors show that clipped Q-learning can penalize out-of-distribution points whose predictions are highly uncertain. They also find that simply increasing the number of Q-networks alongside clipping can substantially outperform existing offline methods on various tasks.

Building on that observation, the paper introduces an ensemble-diversified actor-critic algorithm. It reduces the required ensemble size to one tenth of the naive ensemble while achieving state-of-the-art performance on most evaluated D4RL benchmarks. The results connect uncertainty-based penalties with a more economical ensemble design, supporting improved use of neural-network generalization without imposing an explicit requirement to reproduce the behavior represented in the dataset.
neurips-2021-uncertainty-based-offline-r.tldr: Diversifying Q-network ensembles enables uncertainty-based offline reinforcement learning with one tenth the naive ensemble size and strong reported benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Fine-grained classification distinguishes closely related categories whose visual differences can be subtle. Learning those distinctions usually demands many annotated examples. This paper studies weak-shot learning, where clean examples of base categories support learning new categories from web data. The challenge is to benefit from the web examples while reducing the effect of their noise.

The proposed SimTrans method transfers pairwise semantic similarity from the clean base categories to the new categories. It first trains a similarity network on clean data, then uses the transferred similarity in two strategies for denoising the web training data. An adversarial loss further encourages the similarity network to transfer across the category groups.

Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of both the weak-shot setting and SimTrans. The approach matters because the transferable resource is a learned notion of similarity between examples, which can help assess web data for categories without the same clean supervision. The reported findings support using clean base-category data to improve learning from noisy examples of new, finely distinguished categories.
neurips-2021-weak-shot-fine-grained-clas.tldr: SimTrans transfers semantic similarity from clean base categories to denoise web data for learning new fine-grained categories.
